questions.prompt: In C++20 or later, assuming a 32-bit `unsigned int`, what is printed?
questions.explanation: Zero is not a power of two, so `has_single_bit(0u)` is false, and 8 has a single set bit. `bit_floor(37u)` is the largest power of two not above 37, which is 32, and `bit_ceil(37u)` is the smallest one not below it, which is 64. The option starting with 1 treats zero as a power of two.

questions.prompt: In C++20 or later, assuming a 32-bit `int`, what is printed?
questions.explanation: Since C++20, right shift of a negative signed value is the arithmetic shift, which rounds toward negative infinity, so `-7 >> 1` is -4. Division truncates toward zero, so `-7 / 2` is -3. Before C++20 the shift result was implementation-defined, and the tempting `-3 -3` assumes the two operators agree.

questions.prompt: In C++20 or later, what is printed?
questions.explanation: `rotl` rotates within the width of its argument type, which is 8 bits here, so 0x81 rotated left by one is 0x03 because the top bit wraps around. A negative count rotates the other way, so `rotl(x, -1)` is 0xC0, which is 192. The answer 258 treats the operand as an `int` and lets the bit escape.

questions.prompt: In C++20 or later, assuming a 32-bit `unsigned int`, what is printed?
questions.explanation: The `<bit>` functions look at the width of the exact type, so `countl_zero(std::uint8_t{1})` counts the seven leading zeros of an 8-bit value, and `countl_zero(1u)` counts 31 of a 32-bit value. Unlike the built-in operators, they do not promote a narrow operand to `int` first, which is why `31 31` is wrong.

A `std::uint8_t` operand of `~` is promoted to `int` first, so `~b` complements all 32 bits of the value 15, giving -16. The result is not converted back to 8 bits unless you write `std::uint8_t(~b)`, which is what the tempting answer 240 assumes. There is no overflow, since complementing an `int` is always defined.

questions.prompt: In C++20, assuming a 32-bit `int`, what does this program print?
options: Undefined behavior: the left operand is negative
questions.explanation: Since C++20 a left shift of a signed value is defined modulo 2 to the power of the width, and the two's complement result is read back as signed. For `-1 << 3` that gives -8. Before C++20 a negative left operand made the shift undefined, which is the answer a C++17 reader would give, and it is not a matter of implementation choice now.

questions.prompt: In C++23, assuming a 32-bit `unsigned int`, what is the status of this declaration?
questions.code:
constexpr unsigned x = 1u << 32;

int main() { return 0; }
options: Ill-formed: the initializer is not a constant expression
Well-formed, and `x` has an unspecified value
questions.explanation: A shift whose count is greater than or equal to the width of the promoted left operand has undefined behaviour, even for unsigned types. Undefined behaviour is never allowed in a constant expression, so initializing a `constexpr` variable this way is ill-formed. Shifting out all the bits to leave zero is a common expectation, and it is not what the language says.

questions.prompt: In C++23, assuming a 32-bit `unsigned int`, what is the status of this program?
options: The call has undefined behaviour, so it is not a constant expression and the program is ill-formed
questions.explanation: The next power of two above 0x80000001 would be 2 to the 32nd power, which does not fit in a 32-bit `unsigned int`. [bit.pow.two] makes that case undefined behaviour, and a `constexpr` function may not be used with undefined behaviour in constant evaluation, so the `static_assert` is rejected. Wraparound to 0 is what a hand-written loop would give, but the library function promises nothing of the kind.
